At the end of each sitting, leave a handoff in your journal and last reply: passages still unresolved, practical lessons to carry forward from what you observed and recipes that failed. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Carry forward the conditions of material trials and repairs: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, load, coverage and viewed result; label broader rules as hypotheses. with `scratch: true`; without it they work on the painting.

- The first chunk painted on it sets it up as the painting's canvas was set up: the same
  size, linen and ground. The painting needs its own `canvas{}` first.
- It is a separate canvas: its own palette, brushes, knives, rags and variables (a pile
  knifed for the painting has to be knifed again here), and its own log,
  `paintings/lua/scratch.lua`. Nothing done on it reaches the painting.
- It keeps its own clock. Time spent or waited there (`wait`, `dry()`, `glaze()`) doesn't
  pass for the painting, and the painting's time doesn't pass for it.
- To use what worked, paint it on the painting: the same pile, the same handling.
- `new_scratch: true` (with `scratch: true`) puts the scratch canvas aside and starts a
  fresh one before the chunk runs. The old log stays, as `paintings/lua/scratch-1.lua`, and so on.
- A trial judges a passage only as far as it repeats that passage's conditions: lay the
  underlayer you mean to work over, and let it dry as long as it has on the painting.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

- **Shape the mask like the passage.** Mask wipes start and stop a little
  inside the mask, so a rectangle leaves a frame of the wiped color. If a
  frame shows, wipe along its sides with a path.
- **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
  wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
  clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
  wipes.
- **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
  change what goes on it before painting it again.

## Time

- Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
  lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
  thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
  absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
- **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
  included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
- A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
  campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.

## Finishing

- `save --gallery` (or `save --light az,el`) saves the picture lit on its
  relief, as it would be seen on a wall; plain `save` is color only.

- An unvarnished picture keeps its matte and glossy passages as painted.
  A varnish (where the easel has one) makes it all glossy: darks deepen.

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.

50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set

51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers

events.text:
I need a subject to paint — something like a lit window at dusk, a still life with a blood orange and enamel bowl, a heron in a marsh, or a quiet kitchen at dawn, steering clear of anything too reminiscent of famous paintings. I'm leaning toward a quince on a wintry windowsill, evoking a Spanish bodegón feel.

Actually, I like the idea of a night market fruit stall lit by a bare bulb, with crates of oranges and lemons glowing warm against deep ultramarine-violet night, maybe a striped awning edge and a distant streetlamp, no figures or just a vague silhouette. I'll call it "Fruit stall after dark" and plan a 1000×750mm canvas with a mid-tone warm ground mixing red earth, white, and umber so the citrus can glow against the darker surroundings.

I'm mapping out the composition: the bulb hanging around (330,140) with its glow, the awning underside lit warm across the top-left, crates of oranges, lemons, limes, and pomegranates filling the stall below with little price signs, a dark shadowed interior behind, and to the right a wet night street with a distant streetlamp halo reflecting on the pavement.

Value structure is driven by strong chiaroscuro—brightest at the bulb and nearby fruit, darkest in the night and stall interior. For setup, I'm planning a linen canvas with a lead white, red earth, and raw umber ground applied by knife, then a lean turps lay-in, testing mixes on scratch canvas before starting.

Night3 works as navy, and stall dark gives a warm reddish-brown underpaint. Now I'm moving to the actual lay-in on the painting, starting with the initial drawing.

I'm working out the composition geometry: the awning's valance as a striped red-and-cream scalloped band across the top, a vertical post marking the stall's right edge, and a dark interior wall behind with a hanging bulb and wire placed roughly center.

Below that I'm tiering the fruit crates — lemons and pomegranates in a back row, oranges and limes/mandarins in front, with wooden crate fronts and shadow beneath the table. To the right I'm blocking in the night scene: a silhouetted skyline with a few lit windows, a wet pavement in the foreground, and the street receding toward an eye-level horizon.

Now I'm figuring out the layer sequence for the painting — starting with a thin navy wash for the night zone, a warm dark base for the stall interior with a lighter glow near the bulb, and then building up the crate fronts with the stall's wood tones.

Before diving into color, I think I should rough in a loose gestural drawing in thin burnt sienna first, just to establish the layout and proportions clearly.

I'm rethinking the composition since the current layout feels too grid-like and flat — I want the stall rendered at a slight angle instead of head-on, with rounded fruit mounds in crates rather than boring rectangles, to give it more depth and organic feel.

Working out the perspective math for the stall's front edges and awning valance, converging toward a vanishing point on the right side so the near end reads bigger and the far end recedes naturally.

I'm second-guessing the perspective math and deciding it's overengineered — better to keep a gentle rightward vanishing point for liveliness while letting fruit stay large, and render the heaps as rounded overflowing mounds rather than strict crate rectangles.

Let me recalculate with a shifted vanishing point further right, recomputing key heights for the valance top and bottom, the back and front crate tiers, the table edges, and the ground line, so the perspective convergence feels more natural as the stall extends toward the right edge.

The pavement should run from the near ground line down to where the stall meets it, continuing right into open street space in the foreground. Since the stall front recedes toward a vanishing point off to the right, the street itself must run parallel to that direction, meaning beyond the stall's far end I'd show the street continuing with smaller buildings receding on the left side, while the right side stays hidden behind the stall structure.

The back wall of the stall should read as the ground floor of the building it's set against, with a dark doorway visible, so the stall feels embedded in the facade rather than freestanding. I'm placing a streetlamp near the pavement's edge, its base meeting the curb and its glow a cool, slightly greenish-white tone against the wet road surface.

For the fruit I'm working out two tiers within the stall's interior: a back tier of tilted crates sitting between the valance bottom and a front lip line, and a lower, nearer front tier that's bigger and closer to the viewer, both mapped to shifting y-coordinates as they recede toward the vanishing point.

I'll divide tier assortments by x-position: pomegranates and limes in the back tier, oranges and lemons in the front tier, with the hanging bulb positioned around x≈300 casting its brightest light on the front-tier oranges and falling off gradually toward the edges.

For the first lay-in pass, I'm planning distinct masks: the night sky above the stall (deep navy fading to warm violet-gray glow near the horizon), the dark stall interior lit warmly near the bulb, the striped valance over a mid-warm underpainting, thin local colors for each fruit tier, dark brown for the table front, and a dark blue-gray pavement that will later pick up orange reflections.

I'm working out what sits above the awning line — likely the building facade the stall is attached to, dark with perhaps a lit window, rather than open sky, since the perspective math puts the roofline too high in the frame for sky to show unless the building along the street is shorter past a certain point.

Let me reconsider the geometry: having the stall's building be three storeys tall with its corner edge around x=700-760, then a gap to a cross street or alley beyond, where shorter distant buildings with lit windows let some night sky peek through above them, alongside a streetlamp for added depth.

I've been overplanning this. Time to actually start setting up the vanishing point coordinates and perspective projection function so I can start drawing.

Lay-in (day 1): turps 0.4-0.5 piles, work body/flat 12-16, coverage 2.2-2.5, fill=true, clip=true. Masks are perspective bands via py(y0,x) toward VP (2400,380) — globals VPX,VPY,py,band,STALL_X=662,CORNER_X=770,BX,BY=300,215 (bulb).
Drying observed: thin turps lay-in incl. cadmium piles: still OPEN after 20h, setting/tacky at 3 days, cadmium+alizarin areas tacky at day 7, all dry by day 9. Lead/umber/Prussian sky+wall dry by ~day 4-7.
Scratch: lime = lemon chrome 2 + emerald green 1 (bright lit lime); cad yellow 2 + emerald 1.5 + viridian 0.3 (shadow lime). Night navy = Prussian 1, ultramarine 1, burnt sienna 1.2, bone black 0.3. Ultramarine+alizarin-heavy navy read too purple.
Whole view after lay-in: reads as horizontal colour bands (flag). Wood front band too tall; far buildings same value as sky. Plan: fruit as rounded heaps overflowing lips, crates/cards to break the bands; darker sky top, silhouettes, streetlamp.

Now I'm planning the painting order for the second composition, working back to front and top to bottom. I'm starting with the deep night sky layered with navy, ultramarine, and burnt sienna tones with a warm horizon glow, then adding distant building silhouettes, lit windows, and a streetlamp before moving into the darker upper facade of the main building.

events.name: paint

events.text:
The sky's a bit too pale near the horizon, leaning toward blue hour, but that actually works nicely with the warm stall light and the dark buildings will contrast well against it. Now I'm moving on to the far buildings.

I'm making them dark silhouettes, cooler and lighter than the near facade but still darker than the sky, with an irregular roofline from x=770 to 1000 including a chimney and maybe a tree, and a mixed paint tone of ultramarine, Prussian blue, burnt sienna, lead white, and raw umber. I'll add a few small warm lit windows scattered across them, keeping the cross-street relationship simple for now.

events.name: paint

events.text:
The upper band of the far buildings picked up the wet sky paint underneath, making it too pale and gray rather than reading as a darker silhouette against the sky. Since the lead white sky paint stays open for about twelve hours, I should let it set a bit before going back over it.

For now I'll shift to other passages in this session — the stall's interior back wall, the awning underside, and the valance stripes — then wait a day and come back to correct the far building and tackle the fruit. The fruit is really the main event: I'm thinking of each orange as a rounded form with a dark shadow base, a mid-orange body, a lighter top toward the bulb, and a small specular highlight, built up in loose overlapping filbert dabs rather than careful rendering — first laying in the dark crevice tone across the whole heap, then adding the fruit shapes on top, working smaller toward the back to suggest depth.

Now I'm sketching out the sizing and perspective scaling for the oranges, figuring tiers and rows of fruit shrinking toward the back of the heap, and considering a "touch" approach where a single pressed round dab of body color becomes the fruit itself, followed by a smaller offset dab toward the light source for the highlight — treating each orange almost like one confident brushstroke rather than a multi-step construction.

I'm planning the layering order: dark shadow touch first offset away from the light, then the main body touch offset toward it, then light and highlight touches on top, letting them fuse wet-into-wet for a soft, rounded look. I want to test this on scratch first — painting a small cluster of oranges over a dry dark brown underlayer to see how the dabs blend.

function fruit2(x, y, r, P, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local dx, dy = BX - x, BY - y
  local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); dx, dy = dx/d, dy/d
  local m = ellipse(x, y, r, r*(opts.sq or 0.95)):roughen(r*0.06, r*0.8, math.floor(x*7+y))
  local function lit(px,py_) local nx,ny=(px-x)/r,(py_-y)/r; return clamp(0.35 + 0.9*(nx*dx+ny*dy), 0, 1) end
  work(m, {hand="body", tool={kind="filbert", width=math.max(3,r*0.32)}, piles={
     {P[1], function(px,py_) return math.max(0, 0.7 - lit(px,py_)) * 2 end},
     {P[2], function(px,py_) return 1 - math.abs(lit(px,py_)-0.55)*1.6 end},
     {P[3], function(px,py_) return math.max(0, lit(px,py_)-0.6) * 3 end}},
     length={r*0.4, r*0.9}, coverage=2.2, clip=true, fill=true,
     angle=function(px,py_) return math.atan(py_-y, px-x) + math.pi/2 end})
  if P[4] then
    local b4 = brush{kind="round", width=math.max(2, r*0.18), point=0.6}
    b4:reload(P[4], 0.7)
    local hx, hy = x + dx*r*0.5, y + dy*r*0.5
    b4:stroke({{hx - dy*r*0.08, hy + dx*r*0.08},{hx + dy*r*0.08, hy - dx*r*0.08}}, {pressure={0.6,0.2}})
  end
end
local P = {o_dark, o_body, o_lite, o_hi}
for row=0,2 do
  for i=0,6 do
    local r = 26 - row*3
    local x = 560 + i*r*2.0 + (row%2)*r*0.9 + rand(-4,4)
    local y = 520 - row*r*1.35 + rand(-4,4)
    fruit2(x, y, r, P)
  end
end

events.name: look
events.text: scratch True, crop 500,380,1000,600

These do look like oranges with mottled, crisp edges, but the painting order is off — I did front row first then back rows overlapping, when it should be back-to-front. The light modeling also needs more contrast between lit and shadow sides, and the shadow edges should dissolve into dark crevices rather than staying uniformly crisp.

At 46 minutes for 21 fruits, scaling to ~150 fruits puts me at roughly 5.5 hours total, which seems workable. I want to sharpen the lighting function with stronger contrast between lit and dark piles, add a deeper shadow pile color for the far side, and scale brightness by distance from the bulb so fruit farther away reads darker overall.

Now I'm planning the painting order: back wall, awning underside, and valance first since they sit behind everything, then fruit tier by tier from back to front. For the interior I'm keeping it simple — rough planks warmly lit near the bulb, maybe some hanging bunches and stacked crates behind the fruit.

For the awning underside, since it's seen from below, the canvas stripes would converge toward a different vanishing point than the valance stripes, so I'm defining separate bands for the underside and back wall with distinct color piles — warm ochre-glow near the bulb fading to umber and ultramarine in shadow for the wall, and cream-to-orange glowing tones with red stripe accents for the underside and front valance.

I'll start by blocking in the underside and back wall before tackling the stripe perspective details.

events.text:
The wall feels too flat and even — I want more contrast, brighter near the bulb and darker toward the edges, plus hints of wetness and details like a shelf or hanging bunches later. Now I'm working on the underside of the awning, painting the glowing canvas with stripes running from the valance back toward the wall.

For the perspective, since the stall front recedes toward a right vanishing point, the perpendicular stripes need their own vanishing point far to the left, which lets me draw them as short slanted segments within the band. I'll start with a base layer of warm light near the bulb, then add the red stripe strokes on top.

events.text:
The valance region turned out thinner than I expected, with the stripes only running a shorter band than before. The pattern reads crisp and graphic, almost like a circus tent, but it feels too uniform and evenly lit to be convincing.

Rather than fix that now, I'm stepping back to reconsider the overall composition before tackling the fruit — the big dull wood band could use crates with slats and bright labels, maybe a crate on the ground with pavement reflection, while the large dark side wall might get some texture like a drainpipe or poster without competing too much. For the flat back wall I'm thinking of adding hanging bananas or a scale for visual interest.

Now I'm planning the fruit tiers: pomegranates and limes in the first row, oranges and lemons below, each sized and positioned based on the light falloff from the bulb overhead, with brightness shifting toward shadow as intensity drops across roughly 130 individual fruits.

For crevices between fruits, I'm thinking through sequencing — the lay-in underneath should be dry before fruits go on top, since painting fruits over a wet dark layer would muddy the strokes; painting fruits directly onto the dry mid-tone base and reinforcing dark crevices afterward keeps things cleaner.

I'm also working out the vertical structure between tiers: tier 1's fruit zone, a visible wooden crate-front band with a lit top edge separating it from tier 2, then tier 2's fruit zone beginning lower down, so the crate edge reads as a distinct physical ledge between rows rather than fruit overlapping directly.

I'm now defining the color mixes for each fruit pile — building separate dark, body, highlight, and specular tones for oranges and lemons so each fruit reads with proper shading and light direction.

For limes and pomegranates, I'm setting up similar dark/body/light/highlight pigment combinations, then building an intensity function that maps the lighting value to blend weights across those tiers so the darkest mix dominates in shadow and the highlight only appears where light is strong. I want to test this by painting the first tier of pomegranates on the left and checking how the gradient reads before applying it everywhere.

events.code:
FR = FR or {}
function fruit(x, y, r, P, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local sq = opts.sq or 0.95
  local rot = opts.rot or 0
  local I = opts.I or clamp(bulbnear(x, y, 560)*1.25, 0.05, 1)
  local dx, dy = BX - x, BY - y
  local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); dx, dy = dx/d, dy/d
  local m
  if rot ~= 0 then
    local pts = {}
    for k=0,23 do local a=k/24*2*math.pi; local ex,ey=math.cos(a)*r, math.sin(a)*r*sq
      pts[#pts+1] = {x + ex*math.cos(rot) - ey*math.sin(rot), y + ex*math.sin(rot) + ey*math.cos(rot)} end
    m = poly(pts, true)
  else m = ellipse(x, y, r, r*sq) end
  m = m:roughen(r*0.05, r*0.8, math.floor(x*7+y*3))
  local function lit(px,py_) local nx,ny=(px-x)/r,(py_-y)/r; return clamp(I*(0.45 + 0.85*(nx*dx+ny*dy)), 0, 1) end
  work(m, {hand="body", tool={kind="filbert", width=math.max(2.5,r*0.32)}, piles={
     {P[1], function(px,py_) return math.max(0, 0.5 - lit(px,py_)) * 3 end},
     {P[2], function(px,py_) return math.max(0.05, 1 - math.abs(lit(px,py_)-0.5)*1.7) end},
     {P[3], function(px,py_) return math.max(0, lit(px,py_)-0.58) * 3.5 end}},
     length={r*0.4, r*0.9}, coverage=2.2, clip=true, fill=true,
     angle=function(px,py_) return math.atan(py_-y, px-x) + math.pi/2 end})
  if P[4] and I > 0.35 then
    local b4 = brush{kind="round", width=math.max(1.8, r*0.17), point=0.6}
    b4:reload(P[4], 0.7)
    local hx, hy = x + dx*r*0.5, y + dy*r*0.5*sq
    b4:stroke({{hx - dy*r*0.09, hy + dx*r*0.09},{hx + dy*r*0.09, hy - dx*r*0.09}}, {pressure={0.65,0.15}})
  end
  FR[#FR+1] = {x=x, y=y, r=r, sq=sq, rot=rot}
end

These look more like tomatoes than pomegranates, which need a crown shape. I should add crate structure — tilted wooden boxes with a front lip board partially covering the lower fruit row, plus darker gaps between individual pieces of fruit so they don't appear to float.

My plan: paint dark beds into the remaining tier regions (limes, oranges, lemons) along with the crate front boards now, let that dry, then add fruit over it later so the brightness stays clean. For the pomegranates, I'll touch in dark gaps between the fruit using a mask built from the tier area minus the shrunk fruit ellipses, and later add small crown details and vary the coloring with maroon, crimson, and yellowish-pink patches so they feel less uniform.

I also need to work out the crate fronts — each tier has a front lip board, with a vertical divider where crates sit side by side. I'll start with the interstice darkening on tier 1, then move on to laying dark beds for the other tiers.

Beyond that, the fruit, figure, bulb, and right-side elements like sky and street reflections all need work. I'm also planning to break up the straight tier boundaries by adding overlapping fruit, a crate lip between tiers, a price card tucked into the lemons, and a paper bag, plus a customer figure standing at the counter whose scale I'm working out relative to the plank heights and pavement line.

lsh_g = pile{{"transparent oxide yellow",0.6},{"burnt sienna",0.5},{"ultramarine blue",0.45},{"viridian",0.2}, medium=0.8}
function crescentmask(x, y, r, sq, rot, lx, ly, w)
  local dx, dy = lx - x, ly - y
  local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); dx, dy = dx/d, dy/d
  local ca, sa = math.cos(rot), math.sin(rot)
  local pts = {}
  for k=0,47 do local a=k/48*2*math.pi; local c=math.cos(a); local rr=1+0.13*math.abs(c)^24
    local ex,ey=c*r*rr, math.sin(a)*r*sq; pts[#pts+1]={x+ex*ca-ey*sa, y+ex*sa+ey*ca} end
  local m = poly(pts, true)
  return m, m * mask(function(px,py_) local nx,ny=(px-x)/r,(py_-y)/(r*sq); local t = -(nx*dx+ny*dy); return clamp((t+w)/0.7,0,1) end)
end

end

function coreshadow(x, y, r, sq, rot, lx, ly, pile, load, wid)
  local dx, dy = lx - x, ly - y
  local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); dx, dy = dx/d, dy/d
  local base = math.atan(-dy, -dx)   -- direction away from light
  local ca, sa = math.cos(rot), math.sin(rot)
  local pts = {}
  for k=-3,3 do
    local a = base + k*0.42
    -- point on ellipse at screen angle a, in local coords then inset
    local la = a - rot
    local ex, ey = math.cos(la)*r*0.7, math.sin(la)*r*sq*0.62
    local pr = 0.75 - math.abs(k)*0.2
    pts[#pts+1] = {x + ex*ca - ey*sa, y + ex*sa + ey*ca, math.max(0.05, pr)}
  end
  local b = brush{kind="filbert", width=wid or r*0.35, stiffness=0.4}
  b:load(pile, load or 0.5)
  b:gesture(pts, {wobble=0.3})
end

The figure reads well as a dark silhouette against the lemons, with the bulb giving warmth, but the pomegranates and oranges on the left are still too bright and uniform, competing for attention. I need to apply a darkening glaze there, pushing more falloff toward the left edge and bottom while watching for streaking from the previous glaze pass.

function orb(x, y, r, P, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local sq = opts.sq or 0.95
  local I = opts.I or 1
  local m = ellipse(x, y, r, r*sq):roughen(r*0.03, r*0.8, math.floor(x*7+y*3))
  if opts.cut then m = m - opts.cut end
  local dx, dy = (opts.lx or LX) - x, (opts.ly or LY) - y
  local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); dx, dy = dx/d, dy/d
  local function lit(px,py_) local nx,ny=(px-x)/r,(py_-y)/(r*sq); return clamp(I*(0.35 + 1.0*(nx*dx+ny*dy)), 0, 1) end
  local base = math.atan(dy, dx) + math.pi/2
  work(m, {hand="body", tool={kind="filbert", width=math.max(2.5,r*0.32)}, piles={
     {P[1], function(px,py_) return math.max(0, 0.55 - lit(px,py_)) * 4 end},
     {P[2], function(px,py_) return math.max(0.05, 1 - math.abs(lit(px,py_)-0.55)*2) end},
     {P[3], function(px,py_) return math.max(0, lit(px,py_)-0.6) * 4 end}},
     length={r*0.5, r*1.1}, coverage=2.2, clip=true, fill=true,
     angle=function(px,py_) local nx,ny=(px-x)/r,(py_-y)/r; return base + 0.6*(nx*dx+ny*dy) end})

    b4:touch(hx, hy, {pressure=0.5, drag={-dy*r*0.12, dx*r*0.12}})
  end
  return m
end

events.text:
Day 209 — FINISHING. Reflections and handoff.
Judgement of previously unresolved passages:
- Light centred on bulb: IMPROVED. Graded dglaze (burnt sienna 1, ultra 0.5, medium 0.88) and dglaze2 (+alizarin 0.1, medium 0.8) in nested distance zones from bulb, badger-blended while open; left pomegranates/oranges and counter now fall into shadow. Accept.
- Bulb/glow/wire: DONE (graded wet disc + blend + spirit rag on the overrun). Accept.
- Fruit regularity: PARTLY. Lemons and oranges repainted with smoother rotated forms (lemon()/orb() helpers, medium 0.1-0.12, graded piles); three price cards; a dropped lemon on the pavement. Still row-like heaps, and pomegranates keep the old whorled strokes under glaze. Accepted: in the dark they read as texture and the figure + glow carry the picture; more surgery risked the repeated-repair seams I kept making.
- Customer figure: DONE after one full repaint (slicing repairs kept making seams). Gold rim hairline, red knit hat, bag of oranges. A few yellow flecks remain on the coat (from an unclipped spirit-rag wipe) — accepted, they read as caught light.
- Right side: DONE. Side wall repainted in one pass, windows over DRY building (clean this time), wet road with dragged-and-blended reflections, small streetlamp with rag-lifted halo.
Practical lessons carried forward:
- Repairs in a single shape: repaint the WHOLE passage in one pass; patching slices = seams/blotches.
- Glazes: soft filbert 18, stiffness 0.2, coverage ~0.8-1 per zone, nested masks (coverage can't be a function), badger-blend twice while open. Ultramarine+alizarin glazes go violet.
- Spirit rag (dip 0.6-0.8, pressure 0.75-0.85, several passes) lifts open paint well but isn't clipped: smears lifted colour nearby. Dry rag lifts almost nothing.
- Repeated identical modelling marks (shadow crescents) read as pattern — avoid.
- Locals vanish between chunks: make helpers global (card()).
Heart: fairly happy — the warm cave of light against the blue street, and the woman reaching toward the lemons, is the picture I wanted. Signed lower right.

I've finished *Fruit Stall After Dark* and signed it in the lower right; the painting's clock now reads day 209.

The bulb now does what I wanted: it's painted, with its glow and wire, and it warms the back wall and the nearest fruit. The pomegranates, the left-hand oranges and the counter fall away into shade. A woman in a dark coat and red knit hat stands with her back to us and reaches for the lemons. Her coat has a thin gold edge of light, and she has a string bag of oranges in her other hand. That breaks up the horizontal bands of colour that troubled me last time. To the right, the street is blue: lit windows (repainted over dry paint, so they stayed clean), a small streetlamp, and a wet road with long reflections. A warm spill of light lies on the pavement in front of the counter.

I'm leaving some flaws as they are:
- **Fruit still in rows.** The heaps still sit in rows, though repainted lemons and oranges, three price cards and a dropped lemon help.
- **Pomegranate strokes.** The pomegranates keep the old swirling brushwork under the darkening glaze.
- **Coat flecks.** A few yellow flecks on the coat came from an unclipped rag wipe; they read as caught light.

I accepted these rather than keep patching. The figure taught me that local repairs kept leaving seams, and that a single full repaint worked.

I'm fairly happy with it. The warm stall under the awning against the blue night street, with the woman reaching toward the light, is the picture I set out to make.

The journal has the full handoff and the lessons that still apply, including:
- Repaint a whole passage in one pass rather than patching slices.
- Ultramarine plus alizarin glazes turn violet.
- The spirit-dampened rag isn't clipped, so it smears lifted paint onto nearby areas.
- The same modelling mark repeated across many fruit reads as a pattern.

I've finished **Fruit Stall After Dark**. The painting's clock now reads day 268.

The picture is the same: a striped awning and one bare bulb whose light falls on heaps of pomegranates, oranges, limes and lemons. A woman in a dark coat and red knit hat stands with her back to us, reaching for the lemons, with a bag of oranges in her other hand. To the right is a blue evening street with lit windows, a small streetlamp and a wet road.

This sitting I fixed three things:
- **Right-hand lemons.** They had a brown, leathery-looking crackle left over from an old attempt to wipe off some shading. I painted over the whole patch and repainted the lemons in one pass, then glazed them so they fall into shade away from the bulb. They now read as one clean heap.
- **A hard line across the oranges.** The top of the orange heap had a straight horizontal edge, left behind where an earlier darkening glaze had stopped. Glazing over the line did nothing (I tried twice), because the fruit above it was simply lighter paint. What worked was painting five new oranges across the line and glazing them once dry. The top of the heap is lumpy now and the line is gone.
- **The coat.** A dark glaze deepened it and removed a pale halo along its shadowed side. The gold edge of light stays only on the side facing the bulb.

I'm leaving some flaws as they are:
- **Pomegranates:** they keep their old swirling brushwork under the glaze, which reads as texture in the shadow.
- **Fruit in rows:** some heaps still sit in loose rows.
- **Coat flecks:** a few yellow flecks remain and read as caught light.
- **Plain pavement:** I've left it plain so it stays a quiet ground under the figure.

My heart is happy with it. The light gathers at the bulb, the woman is a dark, quiet shape against the yellow, and the street outside is calm and blue.

The journal has the full handoff. The main new lesson is that a hard edge made by where a shape stops is fixed by painting new shapes across it, not by more glazing. The earlier lessons all still apply.

events.text:
Sitting 5 (day 268 -> 307). Fresh look: the right-hand lemons (x556-663, y362-507) had the brown crackle again. Under the relief light it showed as fine dark broken lines in each lemon, so the day-220 repaint had brought the same fault back.
Scratch diagnosis (scratch canvas, dry gap_body flat 10 cov 2.6 under, 10 d; lemons dried 14 d; then dglaze cov 0.8 + 2 blends): the dark lines show up in the bare lemon() marks even before any glaze. They come from the dry, textured gap_body under them, showing through gaps between thin filbert marks. I tried more coverage (3.5), extra medium (0.3), and an opaque wet underlayer of lemon body in the same chunk (`under=` option). None of them got rid of the lines completely. The wet underlayer made the lines finer and fewer. dglaze laid over that settles into the stroke texture and gives the brown crackle look. Hypothesis (not isolated): the cause is the texture of the dark underlayer combined with thin fruit marks, and a dark burnt-sienna/ultra glaze makes it worse. Knife slab over textured gap_body didn't flatten it (knife rode the ridges).
What I did: covered RLEM again with gap_body (seed 901, dry 13 d). Then 33 + 9 lemons with lemon2() (the old lemon() plus a wet `under` pass of body colour first). Away from the bulb (d>=255) I used new shade piles, les_*: les_body = lemon chrome 2.5, cad yel 0.8, raw sienna 0.5, raw umber 0.15, med 0.15. Each heap gets a lower, warmer value of its own instead of a dark glaze. Rows are rand(-8,8) in y, with more rotation and some end-on lemons. Dried 16 d. Then lglaze (raw sienna 1, transparent oxide yellow 0.5, burnt sienna 0.4, ultra 0.15, medium 0.85) cov 1.0 at d>=225 and 0.9 at d>=290, with 2 blends. That stayed golden and gave no brown crackle. It ran over the green top edge and the post side, so I lifted it with a spirit rag (dip 0.7, pressure 0.8, 3 passes each) while still open; that worked. After 10 d, lglaze2 (lglaze plus more burnt sienna 0.7 and ultra 0.3) cov 1.0/0.8 at d>=275/325, clipped below y357, 2 blends.
Judgement: right lemons IMPROVED and accepted. They read as a heap turning away into warm shade. A faint peel-like texture is left, but no leathery crackle.
Pomegranates' whorled strokes: looked again in the whole view and in crop. ACCEPT. In the dark, under the glaze, they read as texture.
Coat flecks: crop 460-630 x 400-740. ACCEPT; few, and they read as caught light.
Fruit rows and plain pavement: ACCEPT, as before.
New lesson: to put fruit in shade, use a darker body mix rather than a dark glaze over light fruit painted onto a textured dark underlayer. Golden glazes (raw sienna/transparent oxide yellow) sit better on yellows than burnt sienna/ultra does.

Handoff / finish (day 307). Heart: happy. The warm cave of light gathers at the bulb and the woman in the red hat stands dark against the lemons. The right heap now steps back into warm shade, and the blue street stays quiet. Finished.
Practical lessons that still apply: (1) To repair a passage, repaint all of it in one pass, not in slices. (2) A hard edge made by where a shape stops is cured by painting new shapes across it, not by more glaze. (3) Lay glazes as nested distance zones (coverage can't be a function), with a soft filbert 18 at stiffness 0.2, then 2 badger blends while open. Ultramarine with alizarin goes violet. (4) A spirit rag (dip 0.6-0.8, pressure 0.75-0.85) lifts open glaze but isn't clipped. (5) Repeated identical modelling marks read as a pattern. (6) On light fruit over a textured dark underlayer, model shade with darker body piles plus a golden glaze, not a burnt-sienna/ultra glaze. (7) Make helpers global.

I've finished **Fruit Stall After Dark** (painting clock: day 307).

The picture hasn't changed in its main shapes. A striped awning and a single bare bulb light heaps of pomegranates, oranges, limes and lemons. A woman in a dark coat and red knit hat stands with her back to us, reaching for the lemons. To the right is the blue evening street with lit windows, a small streetlamp and wet road.

This sitting I went back to the right-hand lemons. Under raking light the brown, leathery crackle had come back, even after last sitting's repaint. I worked out the cause on the scratch canvas:
- **Where the lines come from:** fine dark lines show through the thin lemon marks from the textured dark undercoat beneath them, before any glaze goes on.
- **What made it worse:** last sitting's dark burnt-sienna/blue shading glaze settled into those lines and turned them into the crackle.
- **What didn't fix it:** heavier coverage, more oil medium and a knife layer over the undercoat. A wet base coat of lemon colour under each lemon made the lines fewer and finer, but didn't remove them.

So I painted the heap over again in a different way:
- **Repaint:** I covered the patch with the dark undercoat and let it dry. Then I painted each lemon over a wet base coat of its own colour.
- **Shade:** the lemons further from the bulb are painted in darker, warmer yellows from the start, instead of being darkened afterwards.
- **Glaze:** once dry, I added two thin golden glazes (raw sienna and transparent oxide yellow) instead of the dark one. Where the first glaze ran onto the limes and the post, I wiped it off with a spirit-dampened rag while it was still wet.

The heap now turns away into warm shade, with a faint peel-like texture where the crackle was. The lemons also sit less in rows.

I've left some flaws as they are:
- **Pomegranates:** they keep their old swirling brushwork under the glaze, which reads as texture in the dark.
- **Coat flecks:** a few yellow flecks remain and read as caught light.
- **Rows:** some fruit heaps elsewhere still sit in loose rows.
- **Plain pavement:** I've left it plain so it stays a quiet ground under the figure.

My heart is happy with it. The light gathers at the bulb, the woman stands dark against the lemons, and the blue street outside stays calm. The journal has the full handoff. The main new lesson is to shade light fruit with darker paint and a golden glaze, not a dark brown glaze over a textured dark undercoat.

drying time before it goes on the painting. `paint`, `look`, `status` and `log` work on it
with `scratch: true`; without it they work on the painting.

- The first chunk painted on it sets it up as the painting's canvas was set up: the same
  size, linen and ground. The painting needs its own `canvas{}` first.
- It is a separate canvas: its own palette, brushes, knives, rags and variables (a pile
  knifed for the painting has to be knifed again here), and its own log,
  `paintings/lua/scratch.lua`. Nothing done on it reaches the painting.
- It keeps its own clock. Time spent or waited there (`wait`, `dry()`, `glaze()`) doesn't
  pass for the painting, and the painting's time doesn't pass for it.
- To use what worked, paint it on the painting: the same pile, the same handling.
- `new_scratch: true` (with `scratch: true`) puts the scratch canvas aside and starts a
  fresh one before the chunk runs. The old log stays, as `paintings/lua/scratch-1.lua`, and so on.
- A trial judges a passage only as far as it repeats that passage's conditions: lay the
  underlayer you mean to work over, and let it dry as long as it has on the painting.

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

events.text:
Sitting 6 (day 307 -> 345). Fresh look: the main passages held. What bothered me was the pavement. The yellow-ochre "spill" scumble in front of the counter read as a muddy mustard smear, and the cast shadow under the boots was a messy violet-yellow blot.
Campaign: repainted the ground in one pass over the dry old pavement. GROUND = NG - (FIG+FIG2):grow(1.5) - the dropped lemon. Used flat 14 with graded piles: spill/wetwarm near the counter, road_dk elsewhere. Coverage 2.8, fill, perspective angle, then 2 blends. The spill pile still went too yellow while wet. A spirit rag (dip 0.8, pressure 0.85, 3x2 passes) didn't lift the yellow; it was mixed into the whole fresh layer. Scraping with a knife (width 28, pressure 1) took the wet layer back to near the dry film, which worked. Then I re-laid wetwarm/road_dk/pave_p only (no spill) at coverage 3 with one blend. Result: a clean, quiet grey-violet ground.
Lesson (hypothesis): a scumbled ochre "light spill" over a dark wet ground reads as yellow mud, not light. Wet pavement mostly reflects what stands on it, so reflect the counter, not the bulb.
Scratch trial (dry pavement, 12 d): reflg (burnt sienna 1, raw umber 0.5, ultra 0.3, transparent oxide yellow 0.3, medium 0.8). Filbert 14, stiffness 0.2, vertical strokes from the base down, length 40-80, pressure 0.7 -> 0.05, then blends vertical and horizontal. Read as a soft wet reflection. On the painting I used irregular spacing (8-20) and lengths (28-75), with reflc (ultra/Prussian/burnt sienna/bone black, medium 0.8) under the blue side wall, and 3 blends. Good: the counter now stands on wet ground.
Also: contact shadows under the boots and the dropped lemon (shadow_p, small filbert), and a kerb line repainted. The signature was lost under the repaint, so I re-signed "MV" lower right (sig pile, round 1.3).
Judgement of previously accepted passages (looked again in whole view and crops):
- Pomegranates' whorled strokes: ACCEPT. They are texture in the shade.
- Coat flecks: ACCEPT. Caught light.
- Fruit rows: ACCEPT. The heaps are lumpy enough at viewing distance, and more surgery risks seams.
- Counter front whorls (old lay-in strokes under the glaze): ACCEPT. They read as wood grain.
- Pavement: IMPROVED (above), no longer "plain".
Uncertain: whether a far subtler warm glaze could add a light spill without going mustard. I didn't try it on the painting.

events.text:
Handoff / finish (day 345). My heart is happy with it. The warm cave of light gathers at the bulb. The woman in the red hat stands dark against the lemons, and now stands on wet ground that holds the counter's reflection. The blue street stays calm.
Practical lessons that still apply:
(1) To repair a passage, repaint all of it in one pass, not in slices.
(2) A hard edge where a shape stops is cured by new shapes across it, not by more glaze.
(3) Lay glazes in nested distance zones (coverage can't be a function), soft filbert 18 at stiffness 0.2, then 2 badger blends while open. Ultra with alizarin goes violet.
(4) A spirit rag lifts thin open glaze but not a freshly mixed body layer. The knife scrape (pressure 1) is the better undo for a fresh body layer.
(5) Repeated identical modelling marks read as pattern.
(6) Model light fruit in shade with darker body piles plus a golden glaze.

Trials on DRY road (scratch, 40 d): (a) opaque warm dashes (rw = orange chrome 1, Naples 0.5, raw sienna 0.3, cad red 0.08), flat 4, unblended -> clean orange; (b) same + badger blend -> OLIVE-GREEN rectangle (blend spreads a thin film of orange over blue); (c) orange/raw sienna glaze (medium 0.75) -> olive. Lesson (fairly firm now): thin warm yellow/orange over the blue-violet greys goes green/mustard — this is also why the old ochre pavement "spill" went mustard. Warm on blue must be opaque and unblended.
Painting: repainted ROADR = m_pave*rect(769,541,240,80) in one pass (road_dk 1 + road_lt graded, flat 12, cov 2.8, fill) -> green gone; dry 10 d. Then refl2() helper: stacked short horizontal dashes, flat 2.2, alternating rw/rwy (cad yel 1, Naples 1, orange chrome 0.4, raw sienna 0.3) and dim rwd (orange chrome 0.6, burnt sienna 0.6, Mars orange 0.4, LW 0.15), width shrinking and gaps widening downward; one per window column, pale lampref dashes under the lamp, dark post_p dashes under the post. Dry 8 d; then reflc glaze nested zones y>570 / y>595 cov 0.5 each + blends, so reflections fade downward (glaze over dry orange dims it to brown-orange, no green). Result: wet street glitters, warm echo of the stall. Keep.

The counter front and pavement lighting look settled, and I'm rejecting that fainter warm glaze since a thin warm layer over blue would shift toward green or mustard. Checking the lit lip reflection and the figure crop near the lamp, things seem close to done — just need to verify the blend hasn't smeared the kerb line or post.
Everything checks out, so I'll finalize the journal judgments and prepare the handoff.

I've finished **Fruit Stall After Dark** (painting clock: day 363).

When I looked fresh, the stall, the woman in the red hat and the pavement all held up. One thing had gone wrong without my noticing: the lit windows' reflections in the wet street on the right had turned an acid green-yellow.

**Why it happened:** I'd originally laid them into the road while its paint was still wet. On the scratch canvas I tested warm strokes on dry road paint:
- Thick warm strokes stayed a clean orange.
- Once softened with a blender, or laid as a thin glaze, the same orange went olive-green.

That also explains why the warm "light spill" I once tried on the pavement went mustard.

**What I did:**
- Repainted that strip of road in one pass and let it dry.
- Laid each window's reflection as a column of short, thick, unblended orange and gold dashes, getting narrower and further apart as they go down.
- Added pale dashes under the streetlamp and dark ones under its post.
- Once those were dry, put a thin cool glaze over the lower part so the reflections fade out downward.

The wet street now glitters faintly and echoes the stall's warmth across the picture without competing with the bulb.

**Flaws I'm leaving as they are:**
- **Pomegranates:** the old swirling brushwork reads as texture in the shade.
- **Coat:** a few yellow flecks read as caught light.
- **Fruit:** some heaps still sit in loose rows.
- **Counter front:** the old swirling strokes read as wood grain.

Last time I wasn't sure whether a fainter warm glaze could suggest light on the pavement. The scratch tests showed it would turn olive, so I didn't try it. The counter's reflection carries that warmth already.

My heart is happy with it. The journal has the updated handoff, with the new lesson: on a blue wet ground, paint warm reflections as thick, unblended dashes over dry paint, because blending them or laying them thin turns them green.
